paragraphs.text: The academic writer Yuval Noah Harari believes we have good cause to feel uneasy about the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) and the role of humans in the workplaces of the future. In his book 21 Lessons for the 21st Century, he warns that there might one day be little need for human labour. He fears the day will come when AI algorithms will outperform humans in all respects that are useful to employers, resulting in widespread job losses throughout the labour market.

Harari’s arguments are based on the plausible assumption that living – and working – is about making decisions. More controversially, he suggests that the processes that underpin our judgements are similar to the way a coffee vending machine goes through a sequence of steps to make coffee. He writes: ‘algorithms controlling vending machines work through mechanical gears and electric circuits, the algorithms controlling humans work through sensations, emotions and thoughts.’ So, everything we do is ultimately algorithmic. And worryingly the algorithms implemented by computers – our workplace rivals – are getting better and better.

But will artificially intelligent algorithms really outperform us in all respects? If David Hodgson’s view is right, we may well have a role. Hodgson, a judge and philosopher, believed we have the edge over machines when it comes to making decisions about ‘incommensurables’. Consider this question: ‘How do you decide between helping a friend, and going to a concert to see a musical you adore?’ It’s difficult, because there is no common standard of measurement for comparing the options. The considerations of duty and desire are incommensurable – different in kind.

Returning to the workplace, there seems to be a whole range of jobs that require reasoned judgements involving incommensurable options. For example, if an architect tries to reconcile the aesthetics of a building’s design against issues relating to the bearing of load, there is incommensurability, because the considerations are of a different kind. How could a robot judge issues of beauty against concerns about how long a building would remain standing? This might be tricky.

Hodgson speculated that the emergence of our ability to weigh up incommensurables enabled our ancestors to make good decisions in response to complex dilemmas. This may give us an evolutionary edge over machines that will, for example, help architects and other workers address the decisions they must make. Harari is surely right to warn about the job disruption that is coming, but if Hodgson is correct, humans will remain more useful in the labour market than Harari imagines.

So how should we prepare for the future? Let’s first look at the types of fears that need addressing. Some alarmists fear a ‘robot apocalypse’ in which robots take control of humans, while others foresee the day of ‘singularity’ when artificial intelligence exceeds human intelligence. Still others warn that income inequality will continue to rise as owners of capital capture more of the benefits of innovations than those who labour for a living.

We should take lessons from the past. Virtually every technological revolution has made workers afraid of losing their jobs. But fighting technology-inspired changes, as the Luddites of early 19th-century England did, rarely works – and can in fact have disastrous consequences. The Luddites were textile workers who feared the advent of automation and so destroyed machines and burned factories. The government eventually suppressed the unrest, killing some workers and jailing many others. But the new technologies that transformed the textile industry continued unabated. While many did lose their jobs, it created many new ones for mechanics and other industrial workers and eventually increased overall productivity.

The important lesson from this episode is that the transition from an agricultural to an industrial economy occurred in the absence of updated policies to govern the transition, which led to more pain for those who were displaced than was necessary. So, what’s needed today aren’t more battle cries, but concerted action by leaders in business, education and government.

From a business perspective, the dominant motivation for introducing new technology is to reduce human labour and the costs associated with it. Robots don’t leave for another job, go on strike or need tea breaks – let alone a salary or benefits. But there is ample historical and current evidence that simply viewing technology as a cost-saving tool leads to overinvestment and weak returns. Just ask the US motor manufacturer General Motors what it got for investing nearly US$50 billion in robots in the 1980s in its futile effort to catch up with Japanese rival Toyota’s more efficient production and labour relations systems. The answer is not much. Instead, General Motors eventually learned from Toyota via a joint venture that the highest return came by integrating new technology with new work practices, which allowed workers to help give wisdom to the machines. The key lesson for business is that it needs to engage workers in designing and deploying new technologies to get the greatest productivity gains.

In terms of education, it is today’s schoolchildren who will be most affected by the AI revolution in coming decades. And while in the past the focus was on the STEM disciplines – science, technology, engineering and maths – industry leaders these days say they need tomorrow’s workforce to be filled with people who can think analytically and creatively, work well together in teams, and adapt readily to near-constant change. And even after people are in the workforce, learning new skills and acquiring new knowledge will need to continue throughout their careers. That means businesses and universities will need to work together, forming new partnerships that ensure the workforce can continue to adapt, and creating a vision and a path forward that everyone can support.

groups.title: Harari and Hodgson’s differing views about the future
content: Developments in artificial intelligence have led to a great deal of {{27}} about the future, and Yuval Harari thinks that this is justified. In his book, 21 Lessons for the 21st Century, Harari argues that everything in our lives involves a series of {{28}} similar to the algorithms which computers use. He explains that while machines use mechanical gears and electrical circuits, our algorithms are based on thoughts and feelings. Harari believes that as AI algorithms become more sophisticated, robots will be able to perform many tasks better than humans, and that this will result in high levels of {{29}}.

David Hodgson took a different view. In his opinion, humans have a noticeable {{30}} over artificial intelligence in relation to “incommensurables”. This means that humans will continue to have some {{31}} in the labour market, despite inevitable advancements in AI.

27.explanation: Feel uneasy tương ứng với concern (lo ngại).

evidence.quote: living – and working – is about making decisions

28.explanation: Harari coi cuộc sống và công việc là quá trình đưa ra decisions, tương ứng choices.

29.explanation: AI vượt con người trong công việc sẽ dẫn tới job losses, tương ứng unemployment.

evidence.quote: we have the edge over machines

30.explanation: The edge over machines có nghĩa lợi thế, tương ứng advantage.

evidence.quote: humans will remain more useful in the labour market than Harari imagines

31.explanation: Theo Hodgson, con người vẫn hữu ích trên thị trường lao động, tức vẫn có value.

evidence.quote: there is no common standard of measurement for comparing the options

32.explanation: Tình huống giữa giúp bạn và đi xem nhạc kịch đòi hỏi cân nhắc duty và desire, hai loại tiêu chí không có chuẩn đo chung.

evidence.quote: How could a robot judge issues of beauty against concerns about how long a building would remain standing?

33.explanation: Ví dụ kiến trúc minh họa khả năng của con người cân nhắc thẩm mỹ và độ bền, một lợi thế so với máy móc.

evidence.quote: This may give us an evolutionary edge over machines

34.explanation: Nếu Hodgson đúng, con người có lợi thế tiến hóa về cân nhắc các lựa chọn không thể so trực tiếp; Harari đã bỏ sót khác biệt này.

evidence.quote: income inequality will continue to rise

35.explanation: Đoạn sáu nêu dự đoán income inequality tiếp tục tăng: khoảng cách giàu nghèo mở rộng.

evidence.quote: the absence of updated policies to govern the transition

36.explanation: Không có chính sách quản lý chuyển đổi đã gây nhiều đau đớn hơn cần thiết; có kế hoạch thì chuyển đổi sẽ thuận lợi hơn.

37.explanation: Bài nói giảm chi phí lao động là động lực phổ biến trong kinh doanh, nhưng không so sánh mức phổ biến giữa sản xuất và ngành khác.

evidence.quote: leads to overinvestment and weak returns

38.explanation: Tác giả dùng General Motors để minh họa đầu tư quá mức và lợi ích thấp; tăng đầu tư vào robot không phải điều được khuyến nghị.

39.explanation: Bài nêu thất bại của General Motors và việc học hỏi Toyota, không nói các công ty ô tô lớn khác lặp lại sai lầm đó.

evidence.quote: while in the past the focus was on the STEM disciplines

40.explanation: STEM là trọng tâm trong quá khứ; hiện nay cần thêm tư duy phân tích, sáng tạo, làm việc nhóm và thích ứng, không phải nhấn mạnh STEM hơn.
